title: Self-Control in Dunedin
text:
In 1972 and 1973, about a thousand babies were born in the city of Dunedin, New Zealand, who would become some of the most closely studied people in the world. The Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study followed nearly all of them from birth into adulthood, with regular, detailed assessments.

In 2011, a team led by Terrie Moffitt and Avshalom Caspi used this data to ask how much childhood self-control matters. Between ages three and eleven, the children's self-control had been rated repeatedly by observers, parents, teachers and the children themselves: how impulsive they were, how easily they got frustrated, how well they could wait their turn and stick with tasks.

By age 32, childhood self-control predicted a remarkable range of outcomes. Children with less self-control were more likely as adults to have physical health problems, to be dependent on drugs or alcohol, to have money troubles and debts, to be single parents and to have criminal convictions. The relationship held along the whole range, not only for the most impulsive children, and it remained after accounting for intelligence and family social class.

The team also studied about 500 pairs of British twins and found that, within the same family, the sibling with lower self-control at age five fared worse by age twelve.
lesson: Self-control learned in childhood pays off across adult life. Helping a child practice patience and persistence is worth the daily effort.
people: Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi and colleagues
source: Moffitt, T. E., Arseneault, L., Belsky, D., et al. (2011). A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(7), 2693-2698.
